sources.title: John K. Hunter, Measure Theory (UC Davis lecture notes)
sources.locator: Chapter 2, “Lebesgue Measure on R^n”, sections 2.1–2.9 complete, printed pp. 9–32 (PDF pp. 13–36), Definition 2.1 through Example 2.37

contents.name: §2.1 Lebesgue outer measure
Definition 2.1 (n-dimensional closed rectangle and its volume)
Definition 2.2 (outer Lebesgue measure by countable rectangle covers)
Example 2.3 (the rationals in [0,1] have outer measure zero)
Theorem 2.4 (outer Lebesgue measure vanishes at the empty set, is monotone and is countably subadditive)
§2.2 Outer measure of rectangles
Lemma 2.5 (the volume of a rectangle is the sum of the volumes of a product subdivision)
Proposition 2.6 (volume is additive over a finite almost disjoint decomposition and subadditive over a finite cover)
Proposition 2.7 (the outer measure of a rectangle equals its volume)
§2.3 Carathéodory measurability
contents.reason: Hunter's §2.3 is the Caratheodory measurability test and the sigma-algebra theorem built on it; both are published on the preceding pair, as def-caratheodory-measurable-set (the test $\mu^*(A)=\mu^*(A\cap E)+\mu^*(A\setminus E)$ for every $A\subseteq X$) and thm-caratheodory-outer-measure-theorem. This page cites them rather than minting a second definition of the same notion.

contents.name: Definition 2.8 (Carathéodory measurable set for an abstract outer measure)
contents.reason: Published on disk as def-caratheodory-measurable-set, with the quantifier over every test set $A$ stated as part of the definition; this page cites it rather than restating the test.

contents.name: Theorem 2.9 (the Carathéodory measurable sets form a sigma-algebra and the outer measure restricts to a measure on them)
contents.reason: Published on disk as thm-caratheodory-outer-measure-theorem, in the form "for an outer measure on $X$, the Caratheodory measurable subsets form a sigma-algebra, and the restriction of the outer measure to it is a complete measure"; this page consumes it to obtain the Lebesgue sigma-algebra rather than reproving the abstract statement.

contents.name: Definition 2.10 (Lebesgue measurable subset of R^n)
Proposition 2.11 (every rectangle is Lebesgue measurable)
§2.4 Null sets and completeness
Proposition 2.12 (a set of outer measure zero is measurable, so Lebesgue measure is complete)
Definition 2.13 (a subset of R^n has Lebesgue measure zero)
Example 2.14 (the standard Cantor set has measure zero)
Example 2.15 (the x-axis has measure zero in R^2)
§2.5 Translational invariance
Proposition 2.16 (outer measure and measurability are unchanged by translation)
Example 2.17 (a transversal of the cosets of Q in R is not Lebesgue measurable)
contents.reason: The Vitali construction and its exact choice cost are the declared subject of the next pair in this track, which also owns Bernstein sets and the Solovay ledger; building it here would take the page's only use of a choice principle beyond countable choice.

contents.name: §2.6 Borel sets
Definition 2.18 (the Borel sigma-algebra on R^n)
Remark 2.19 (the Borel sigma-algebra is not described constructively by the generation from open sets)
Proposition 2.20 (every open set in R^n is a countable union of almost disjoint cubes)
Proposition 2.21 (the Borel sigma-algebra is generated by the rectangles, so every Borel set is Lebesgue measurable)
Example 2.22 (the Cantor function carries a null set onto a set of positive measure, giving a Lebesgue measurable set that is not Borel)
contents.reason: The explicit Cantor-function witness needs continuity of that function, which is not available at this point in the reading order, and the next pair in this track owns the explicit route; this page refutes the Borel-equals-Lebesgue claim by a counting argument instead.

contents.name: §2.7 Borel regularity
Theorem 2.23 (outer regularity by open sets and inner regularity by closed and compact sets)
Theorem 2.24 (measurability is equivalent to approximation from outside by open sets)
Theorem 2.25 (measurability is equivalent to approximation from inside by closed sets)
Definition 2.26 (G-delta and F-sigma sets)
Theorem 2.27 (a measurable set is a G-delta minus a null set and an F-sigma plus a null set)
Theorem 2.28 (the Lebesgue sigma-algebra is the completion of the Borel sigma-algebra)
§2.8 Linear transformations
Lemma 2.29 (an oblique rectangle containing a finite almost disjoint collection of cubes bounds their total volume)
contents.reason: This is an internal step of Hunter's direct geometric proof of orthogonal invariance; this page proves orthogonal invariance as a corollary of the determinant formula, which is obtained from the uniqueness theorem, so the lemma supports no statement that is left unbuilt.

contents.name: Proposition 2.30 (an oblique rectangle is approximated within epsilon by a finite union of cubes)
contents.reason: Like Lemma 2.29 this is a step of the oblique-rectangle route to orthogonal invariance and has no standalone statement worth a page item; the theorem it serves is built here by the uniqueness route, so nothing it supports is lost.

contents.name: Theorem 2.31 (an orthogonal transformation preserves Lebesgue outer measure)
Proposition 2.32 (a diagonal linear transformation scales measure by the product of the absolute entries)
Theorem 2.33 (a linear transformation scales Lebesgue measure by the absolute determinant)
§2.9 Lebesgue-Stieltjes measures
contents.reason: The correspondence between increasing right-continuous functions and Borel measures finite on compacta is the declared subject of a later pair in this track, and building it here would duplicate that page's whole development.

contents.name: Theorem 2.34 (an increasing right-continuous F determines a Borel measure with mu_F((a,b]) = F(b) - F(a))
contents.reason: This is the existence half of the Lebesgue-Stieltjes correspondence and belongs with its uniqueness half and with the distribution-function dictionary, none of which this page's remit covers.

contents.name: Example 2.35 (F(x) = x recovers Lebesgue measure on R)
contents.reason: The example is the specialisation of Theorem 2.34 and is meaningless before that theorem exists; the identification of the case F(x)=x with lambda_1 is the natural first example on the Lebesgue-Stieltjes page.

contents.name: Example 2.36 (a jump function gives a Dirac measure)
contents.reason: A Dirac measure is already published as def-dirac-measure, and exhibiting it as a Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure requires Theorem 2.34, so the example belongs where that theorem is proved.

contents.name: Example 2.37 (the Cantor function gives a measure assigning full mass to the Cantor set)
contents.reason: The singular Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure carried by the Cantor function needs the Cantor function's continuity and monotonicity together with Theorem 2.34, and it is the standard example of a measure singular with respect to lambda_1, which belongs with the decomposition theory.

sources.title: Terence Tao, An Introduction to Measure Theory (GSM 126)
sources.locator: §1.1.1 “Elementary measure”, printed pp. 2–8 (PDF pp. 18–24), Exercise 1.1.1 through Exercise 1.1.4; and §1.2 “Lebesgue measure” complete, printed pp. 17–46 (PDF pp. 33–62), Exercise 1.2.1 through Remark 1.2.19; and §1.6.1 “The Lebesgue differentiation theorem in one dimension” and §1.6.2 “The Lebesgue differentiation theorem in higher dimensions” complete, printed pp. 136–155 (PDF pp. 152–171), Exercise 1.6.5 through Exercise 1.6.27, stopping before §1.6.3

contents.name: §1.1.1 Elementary measure
Exercise 1.1.1 (Boolean closure: elementary sets are closed under union, intersection, difference and symmetric difference)
Lemma 1.1.2 (Measure of an elementary set: a finite disjoint box decomposition exists and the volume sum is independent of it)
Exercise 1.1.2 (two box partitions of an elementary set admit a mutual grid refinement)
Remark 1.1.3 (the naive limit of grid counts as a candidate measure)
Exercise 1.1.3 (Uniqueness of elementary measure under non-negativity, finite additivity and translation invariance)
Exercise 1.1.4 (elementary measure is multiplicative on products of elementary sets)
contents.reason: The product formula for elementary sets is the finite-dimensional shadow of the product measure construction, and the page that owns products, Tonelli and Fubini is where the general statement and its measurability hypotheses belong.

contents.name: §1.2.1 Properties of Lebesgue outer measure
Exercise 1.2.1 (a countable union or intersection of Jordan measurable sets need not be Jordan measurable)
contents.reason: The union half is published on disk as cex-rational-points-in-unit-square-have-no-jordan-content: the rational points of $[0,1]^2$ are a countable union of Jordan measurable singletons whose boundary is the whole square, so the union is not Jordan measurable, and the intersection half is the complement of that same witness inside the square. This page records instead the exact comparison between Jordan content and Lebesgue measure.

contents.name: Exercise 1.2.2 (uniformly bounded Riemann integrable functions with a non-integrable pointwise limit)
contents.reason: The failure of the Riemann integral under pointwise limits is a statement about integrals, not about measure, and it is the motivating example of the page comparing the Riemann and Lebesgue integrals.

contents.name: Example 1.2.1 (a countable set has Lebesgue outer measure zero although its Jordan outer content can be positive)
Remark 1.2.3 (Littlewood's first principle: a measurable set is almost open)
Exercise 1.2.3 (The outer measure axioms: empty set, monotonicity, countable subadditivity)
Remark 1.2.4 (outer measure on an abstract set, and the Carathéodory construction)
contents.reason: Published on disk as def-outer-measure (a function on the whole power set that vanishes at the empty set, is monotone and is countably subadditive), together with def-outer-measure-induced-by-a-premeasure for the construction from a premeasure; this page cites both rather than restating them.

contents.name: Lemma 1.2.5 (Finite additivity for positively separated sets)
contents.reason: Published on disk as def-metric-outer-measure ($\mu^*(A\cup B)=\mu^*(A)+\mu^*(B)$ whenever $A,B$ are nonempty with $d(A,B)>0$), with Caratheodory’s criterion as prop-closed-sets-are-caratheodory-measurable-for-metric-outer-measures. This page obtains measurability of the Borel sets from the extension theorem instead, so the separated-additivity route is cited and not rebuilt.

contents.name: Exercise 1.2.4 (two disjoint closed sets, one compact, are positively separated, and compactness cannot be dropped)
contents.reason: No published item states this exercise at its own strength. ex-distance-to-a-set-is-attained-on-a-compact-set proves positive distance for two disjoint COMPACT sets, and cex-set-distance-is-not-a-metric supplies the two disjoint closed sets of the line at distance zero; the compact-plus-closed strengthening between them is carried by neither. Its natural home, compactness-in-metric-spaces, is already published, so placing it is an owner decision rather than a page this run can defer to. Nothing here needs it: this page separates compact from closed sets through Heine-Borel and sigma-compactness directly, never through a separation estimate.

contents.name: Lemma 1.2.6 (the Lebesgue outer measure of an elementary set is its elementary measure)
Remark 1.2.7 (countable sets are null, which reproves that R^d is uncountable)
Remark 1.2.8 (a bounded open set and a compact set that are not Jordan measurable)
Lemma 1.2.9 (the outer measure of a countable union of almost disjoint boxes is the sum of their volumes)
Remark 1.2.10 (two almost disjoint box decompositions of the same set have equal volume sums)
Exercise 1.2.5 (a countable union of almost disjoint boxes has Lebesgue outer measure equal to its Jordan inner measure)
contents.reason: Jordan inner measure of an unbounded or non-Jordan set is an extension of the published inner content that the library has not defined, and defining it only to state this identity would add a notion no later page uses.

contents.name: Lemma 1.2.11 (an open set is a countable union of almost disjoint closed cubes, by the dyadic mesh)
Lemma 1.2.12 (Outer regularity of Lebesgue outer measure for an arbitrary set)
Exercise 1.2.6 (inner approximation by open subsets fails)
§1.2.2 Lebesgue measurability
Lemma 1.2.13 (Existence of Lebesgue measurable sets: open, closed and null sets are measurable, and the family is closed under complement and countable unions and intersections)
Remark 1.2.14 (the measurable sets form a sigma-algebra)
Exercise 1.2.7 (Criteria for measurability: open, closed, G-delta and F-sigma approximations)
Exercise 1.2.8 (every Jordan measurable set is Lebesgue measurable)
Exercise 1.2.9 (Middle thirds Cantor set: it is compact, uncountable and null)
Exercise 1.2.10 ([0,1) is not a countable disjoint union of closed intervals)
contents.reason: The statement is a point-set topology fact about the line proved by a Baire or connectedness argument and carries no measure content; it is unrelated to every theorem this page builds and belongs with the published topology of R if it is ever wanted.

contents.name: Lemma 1.2.15 (The measure axioms: Lebesgue measure vanishes at the empty set and is countably additive)
Exercise 1.2.11 (Monotone convergence theorem for measurable sets: continuity from below)
Exercise 1.2.12 (empty set and countable additivity imply monotonicity and countable subadditivity)
Exercise 1.2.13 (dominated convergence for sets, and its failure without a dominating set of finite measure)
Exercise 1.2.14 (every set is contained in a measurable set of exactly its outer measure)
Exercise 1.2.15 (Inner regularity by compact subsets)
Remark 1.2.16 (inner and outer regularity as the definition of a Radon measure)
contents.reason: Radon measures on a locally compact Hausdorff space, and the representation theorem that motivates them, are the declared subject of a later pair in this track.

contents.name: Exercise 1.2.16 (Criteria for finite measure: nine equivalent approximation conditions)
Exercise 1.2.17 (Carathéodory criterion, one direction: testing against elementary sets and against boxes)
Exercise 1.2.18 (Lebesgue inner measure of a bounded set, and measurability as equality of inner and outer measure)
contents.reason: Inner measure earns its keep only where it can differ from outer measure, and exhibiting that gap needs a non-measurable set, which the next pair in this track owns together with the Bernstein set for which the gap is as large as possible.

contents.name: Exercise 1.2.19 (measurability is equivalent to being a G-delta minus a null set and to being an F-sigma plus a null set)
Remark 1.2.17 (the trade-off between the strength of the approximation and the structure obtained)
Exercise 1.2.20 (Translation invariance of Lebesgue measurability and measure)
Exercise 1.2.21 (Change of variables: a linear image is measurable with measure scaled by the absolute determinant)
Exercise 1.2.22 (outer measure of a product is submultiplicative, and the product of measurable sets is measurable with the product measure)
contents.reason: The product formula for Lebesgue measurable factors is the base case of the product measure construction and needs the completed product, which is the declared subject of the Fubini-Tonelli pair.

contents.name: Exercise 1.2.23 (Uniqueness of Lebesgue measure from the empty set, countable additivity, translation invariance and normalisation)
Exercise 1.2.24 (Lebesgue measure as the metric completion of elementary measure on a fixed elementary set)
contents.reason: The metric packaging needs a complete metric on equivalence classes of sets modulo null symmetric difference, an object no later page in this track uses; the mathematical content, that a measurable set of finite measure is approximable by an elementary set in outer measure, is included as a clause of the Littlewood characterisations, and the measure-theoretic completion statement is included separately.

contents.name: Exercise 1.2.25 (a continuously differentiable curve in R^d has measure zero for d at least two, and the C^1 hypothesis cannot be dropped)
contents.reason: The space-filling-curve half needs Peano's construction and the positive half needs the C^1 mean value estimate on a curve; the Lipschitz image theorem this page does use is already published, and the curve statement itself is a differentiation fact whose home is the covering and differentiation pair.

contents.name: Proposition 1.2.18 (there is a non-Lebesgue-measurable subset of [0,1])
contents.reason: The Vitali set is the declared subject of the next pair in this track, which also fixes the exact choice principle used; this page is a theorem of ZF plus countable choice throughout and would lose that if the construction were placed here.

contents.name: Exercise 1.2.26 (Lebesgue outer measure is not finitely additive)
contents.reason: The failure of finite additivity on arbitrary sets is exactly the phenomenon a non-measurable set exhibits, so the witness and the false statement recording it belong with the non-measurable material.

contents.name: Exercise 1.2.27 (the projection of a Lebesgue measurable planar set need not be measurable)
contents.reason: A measurable planar set with a non-measurable projection is built from a non-measurable subset of the line, which this page does not have, and the statement is also the standard warning attached to the composition rules for measurable functions.

contents.name: Remark 1.2.19 (with the axiom of choice, no translation-invariant countably additive extension of Lebesgue measure to all subsets of R exists)
§1.2.3 Non-measurable sets
contents.reason: The whole subsection is the subject of the next pair in this track, which the design assigns the Vitali, Bernstein and Sierpinski constructions and the choice ledger.

contents.name: Theorem 1.6.11 (Lebesgue differentiation theorem, one-dimensional case)
contents.reason: Differentiating the indefinite integral needs the Lebesgue integral, and this page stops at the construction of $\lambda_n$ before any integral is defined; the one-dimensional differentiation theorem is the opening result of the maximal-function pair.

contents.name: Exercise 1.6.5 (the indefinite integral of an absolutely integrable function is continuous)
contents.reason: Continuity of $x\mapsto\int_{(-\infty,x]}f$ is a statement about the Lebesgue integral of an absolutely integrable function, and neither the integral nor absolute integrability exists before the integral pair.

contents.name: Theorem 1.6.12 (Lebesgue differentiation theorem, second formulation)
contents.reason: The one-sided averaged form $\lim_{h\to0^+}\frac1h\int_{[x,x+h]}f=f(x)$ almost everywhere restates the differentiation theorem for averages and rests on the same absent integral; it is the form the maximal-function pair establishes first.

contents.name: Exercise 1.6.6 (Theorem 1.6.11 follows from Theorem 1.6.12)
contents.reason: This is the deduction of one formulation of the differentiation theorem from the other, and it has no content once neither formulation is available; it travels with the two theorems it connects.

contents.name: Proposition 1.6.13 (translation is continuous in $L^1$)
contents.reason: Continuity of $h\mapsto f_h$ needs the $L^1$ norm, which the library reaches with the $L^p$ spaces. The set-level counterpart is built here as thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant, and that is all this page uses.

contents.name: Remark 1.6.14 (running the density argument a second time on a nicer subclass)
contents.reason: Methodological commentary on organising the density argument for the differentiation theorem; it asserts nothing that can be built independently of that theorem.

contents.name: Exercise 1.6.7 (the convolution of an absolutely integrable with an essentially bounded function is well defined, bounded and continuous)
contents.reason: Convolution is an integral of a product and cannot be written before the Lebesgue integral exists. Its smoothing property is exactly the route Tao then takes to Steinhaus, whereas this page reaches Steinhaus through the dyadic-cube density estimate instead.

contents.name: Exercise 1.6.8 (Steinhaus theorem)
Exercise 1.6.9 (measurable additive homomorphisms $\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb C$ are continuous, and are exactly the linear forms)
contents.reason: Automatic continuity of a measurable homomorphism is a statement about characters rather than about the measure, and its home is the locally compact abelian group development; the Steinhaus theorem this page proves is the input it will use, not a consequence of it.

contents.name: Remark 1.6.15 (the density argument gives qualitative rather than quantitative convergence)
contents.reason: The remark motivates the maximal inequality by observing that the density argument supplies no rate of convergence; it is commentary attached to the differentiation theorem with no standalone claim.

contents.name: Lemma 1.6.16 (one-sided Hardy-Littlewood maximal inequality)
contents.reason: The weak-type bound on the one-sided maximal function is stated for an absolutely integrable $f$ and is the central estimate of the maximal-function pair; it is not expressible before the integral is defined.

contents.name: Lemma 1.6.17 (rising sun lemma)
contents.reason: The rising sun lemma is about a continuous real function on a compact interval and the intervals on which it fails to dominate to the right; it is the covering tool of the monotone-differentiation pair, and no result on this page is proved by it.

contents.name: Remark 1.6.18 (the picture behind the name of the rising sun lemma)
contents.reason: An explanation of the hillside picture behind the previous lemma, carrying no mathematical assertion of its own; it belongs beside the lemma it names.

contents.name: Exercise 1.6.10 (every open subset of $\mathbb R$ is an at most countable union of disjoint non-empty open intervals whose endpoints lie outside it)
contents.reason: Published on disk as thm-open-subsets-of-r-structure, "every open subset of $\mathbb R$ is a countable disjoint union of open intervals, namely its order components". This page builds the $\mathbb R^n$ dyadic-cube analogue it actually needs, as thm-open-subsets-of-rn-are-countable-disjoint-unions-of-dyadic-cubes.

contents.name: Exercise 1.6.11 (two-sided Hardy-Littlewood maximal inequality)
contents.reason: The two-sided form of the same weak-type bound, deduced from the one-sided lemma; it needs the integral and belongs beside the inequality it is deduced from.

contents.name: Exercise 1.6.12 (rising sun inequality)
contents.reason: The rising sun inequality bounds the measure of a superlevel set of the one-sided signed maximal function by an integral over that set; it is the sharpened companion of the rising sun lemma and waits for the same pair.

contents.name: Exercise 1.6.13 (the two sides of Lemma 1.6.16 are in fact equal)
contents.reason: This upgrades the one-sided maximal inequality to an equality and cannot be stated before that inequality is; it is a refinement for whichever pair proves the inequality.

contents.name: Theorem 1.6.19 (Lebesgue differentiation theorem in general dimension)
contents.reason: The $\mathbb R^d$ differentiation theorem averages an absolutely integrable function over shrinking balls, so it needs both the integral and the maximal inequality; it is the target result of the maximal-function pair.

contents.name: Exercise 1.6.14 (local integrability, and the differentiation theorem for locally integrable functions)
contents.reason: Local integrability is a property of the Lebesgue integral over balls and is introduced with the integral; the weakening of the differentiation theorem it supports follows that page.

contents.name: Exercise 1.6.15 (averages over subsets of comparable measure inside shrinking balls converge at a Lebesgue point)
contents.reason: The statement is about Lebesgue points of a locally integrable function, a notion defined by integral averages. It is one of the two inputs Tao uses for Exercise 1.6.25, and this page instead reaches that exercise’s conclusion by Tao’s own alternative route through outer regularity.

contents.name: Exercise 1.6.16 (the general-dimension differentiation theorem for continuous functions)
contents.reason: The dense-subclass case of Theorem 1.6.19, which is a step inside that theorem’s proof rather than a result this page could carry on its own.

contents.name: Theorem 1.6.20 (Hardy-Littlewood maximal inequality)
contents.reason: The $\mathbb R^d$ weak-type bound with constant $C_d$ is the quantitative heart of the differentiation theorem and is stated for absolutely integrable functions; the pair named for the maximal function proves it.

contents.name: Remark 1.6.21 (the Hardy-Littlewood maximal function $Mf$)
contents.reason: Names and discusses the object the preceding inequality bounds; it introduces no separate claim and travels with that inequality.

contents.name: Exercise 1.6.17 (the maximal inequality implies the general-dimension differentiation theorem by the density argument)
contents.reason: This is the density-argument deduction joining Theorem 1.6.20 to Theorem 1.6.19 and has no content apart from those two theorems.

contents.name: Lemma 1.6.22 (Vitali-type covering lemma for a finite collection of open balls)
contents.reason: The finite ball-selection lemma with its $3^d$ dilation is a covering statement this page never needs: its covering work is done by dyadic cubes, which are disjoint by construction and need no selection step.

contents.name: Exercise 1.6.18 (recasting the greedy ball selection as a formal induction)
contents.reason: A note on formalising the greedy algorithm inside the covering lemma’s proof; it is a presentation exercise for that lemma and states nothing further.

contents.name: Remark 1.6.23 (the actual Vitali covering lemma, and the family of related covering lemmas)
contents.reason: Distinguishes Tao’s finite version from Vitali’s own covering theorem, which is the named result of the pair that owns covering arguments; no statement is proved at this heading.

contents.name: Exercise 1.6.19 (improving the maximal-inequality constant from $3^d$ to $2^d$)
contents.reason: A quantitative improvement of the constant in an inequality this page does not state, so it cannot precede the inequality it sharpens.

contents.name: Remark 1.6.24 (the optimal constant $C_d$, and Melas’ value for $d=1$)
contents.reason: Reports what is known about the sharp constant in the Hardy-Littlewood inequality, including the one-dimensional value; it is bibliography attached to that inequality.

contents.name: Exercise 1.6.20 (dyadic maximal inequality)
contents.reason: The dyadic-cube form of the maximal inequality. This page does build the dyadic-cube machinery such a proof would use, but the inequality itself bounds averages of an integrable function, so it waits for the integral.

contents.name: Exercise 1.6.21 (Besicovitch covering lemma in one dimension)
contents.reason: Selecting a subfamily of intervals with bounded overlap is a second covering theorem, sharper than Vitali’s in the bounded-multiplicity sense; it belongs with the covering pair and nothing here uses it.

contents.name: Exercise 1.6.22 (Hardy-Littlewood maximal inequality for an inner regular Borel measure on $\mathbb R$)
contents.reason: The generalisation of the one-dimensional maximal inequality with Lebesgue measure replaced by an inner regular locally finite Borel measure; it presupposes both the Lebesgue case and integration against a general measure.

contents.name: Exercise 1.6.23 (Cousin’s theorem)
contents.reason: Published on disk as thm-cousins-lemma-for-gauges, "every gauge on a compact interval admits a fine tagged partition", with ex-cousins-lemma-gives-heine-borel-on-an-interval recording the Heine-Borel direction Tao’s hint runs the other way.

contents.name: Exercise 1.6.24 (almost every point of a measurable set is a point of density for it)
contents.reason: The Lebesgue density theorem. This page proves only the far weaker statement that some dyadic cube is filled to a prescribed proportion, which is what Steinhaus needs and what outer regularity alone supplies; the density theorem itself needs the differentiation theorem.

contents.name: Exercise 1.6.25 (a measurable set of positive measure fills all but $\varepsilon$ of some cube; an alternative proof avoiding the differentiation theorem; and a second proof of the Steinhaus theorem)
Exercise 1.6.26 (a compact set of positive measure meeting every interval in less than its length, and a measurable set meeting every interval in more than nothing and less than its length)
contents.reason: Part (i)’s construction is the dense open subset of small measure this page builds as ex-a-dense-open-subset-of-the-unit-interval-of-small-measure, but the stated conclusions are about the densities of a set in every interval at once, which is the sharpness discussion belonging beside the density theorem.

contents.name: Exercise 1.6.27 (approximations to the identity: good kernels, and convergence of $f*P_t$ at Lebesgue points)
contents.reason: Good kernels are defined by a normalised integral and act by convolution, neither available here; approximate-identity theory is the declared subject of the convolution pair.

sources.title: Eric A. Carlen, Notes on Lebesgue Measure on R^n and S^{n-1} for Math 501 (Rutgers)
sources.locator: §1 “Construction of Lebesgue measure on R^n” (pp. 1–5), §2 (pp. 5–6) and §3 (pp. 6–9), Theorem 1.1 through Theorem 3.4, stopping before §4 on the sphere

contents.name: §1 Construction of Lebesgue measure on R^n (the elementary family E_n of half-open rectangles and the algebra A_n of finite disjoint unions)
Theorem 1.1 (rho_n is a semi-finite premeasure on A_n, continuous at the empty set)
Definition 1.2 (Lebesgue outer measure and Lebesgue measure as the Carathéodory extension)
Theorem 1.3 (the Carathéodory extension of a premeasure)
contents.reason: Published on disk as thm-caratheodory-extension-theorem, assuming countable choice, together with the uniqueness and completion clauses this page consumes.

contents.name: Proposition 1.4 (sigma(A_n) is the Borel sigma-algebra on R^n)
Theorem 1.5 (Lebesgue measure is inner and outer regular on the Lebesgue measurable sets)
Theorem 1.6 (Approximation of a measurable set of finite measure by a finite union of rectangles)
Theorem 1.7 (L^1 of Lebesgue measure is separable and the smooth compactly supported functions are dense in it)
contents.reason: Density of the smooth compactly supported functions and separability of L^1 are statements about an integral and a normed space, neither of which exists at this point in the reading order; the pair on density, separability and convolution owns them.

contents.name: Theorem 2.1 (the change of variables formula for an integral under a measurable map, the push-forward measure)
contents.reason: The push-forward of a measure is defined without the integral, but the theorem as stated is about integrals of nonnegative measurable functions, so it belongs with the construction of the integral.

contents.name: Theorem 2.2 (Uniqueness of measures agreeing on a generating pi-system with a finite-measure exhaustion)
Theorem 2.3 (Translation invariance of Lebesgue measure, via the push-forward and the uniqueness theorem)
Theorem 3.1 (for invertible linear T, T pushes Lebesgue measure to |det T|^{-1} times itself)
Theorem 3.2 (Rotation invariance of Lebesgue measure for an orthogonal transformation)
Theorem 3.3 (Rotation invariance of Lebesgue measure, restated for the integral)
Theorem 3.4 (Transformation of Lebesgue measure under the dilation by t)

sources.title: Steinhaus theorem (Wikipedia)
sources.locator: the whole article: Statement, Proof, Corollary, Applications, See also, Notes, References

contents.name: Statement (the difference set of a set of positive Lebesgue measure contains an open neighbourhood of the origin)
Proof (via the Lebesgue density theorem, and the alternative regularity argument)
Corollary (a measurable proper subgroup of the additive reals has measure zero)
Steinhaus-Weil theorem (for a locally compact group and left Haar measure, AA^{-1} contains a neighbourhood of the unit)
contents.reason: Haar measure on a locally compact group is not built anywhere in this library, and the Euclidean case this page proves is the only instance its remit covers.

contents.name: Lebesgue density theorem (cited in the proof)
contents.reason: The density theorem is the declared subject of the maximal-function and differentiation pair in this track; this page proves Steinhaus by the weaker dyadic-cube density estimate it can establish directly, which is recorded as its own lemma.

contents.name: Applications (Falconer's conjecture and distance sets)

Corollary 1.2 (a measurable proper subgroup of $(\mathbb R,+)$ is null)
Definition 1.3 ($X_A:=\{x\in\mathbb R: A+xA=\mathbb R\}$ for a subgroup $A$ of $(\mathbb R,+)$)
contents.reason: The set of dilation parameters that make a subgroup fill the line is the paper’s own object of study and appears nowhere else; it has no role in constructing Lebesgue measure and no page of this library is about it.

contents.name: Question 1 (for a subgroup, subring or subfield $A$ of $\mathbb R$, is there an $x$ with $A+xA=\mathbb R$, and how large must $A$ then be?)
contents.reason: This is the open question the paper is written to attack, not an established result; the library builds settled mathematics, and a question has no statement to prove here or anywhere.

contents.name: Theorem 1.4 (there is an $F_\sigma$ subgroup $A$ of $(\mathbb R,+)$ with $\dim_H(A)\le 1/2$ and $X_A\ne\varnothing$)
contents.reason: A 2025 research theorem about Hausdorff dimension of subgroups of the reals; the library has not reached Hausdorff measure, and a current research result is not material this run establishes.

contents.name: Theorem 1.5 (under the continuum hypothesis there is a subgroup $A$ with $\dim_H(A)=0$ and $X_A=\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q$)
contents.reason: A research theorem proved under the continuum hypothesis, combining Hausdorff dimension with a genericity construction; neither the dimension theory nor the independence machinery it uses is available, and it is far outside a page constructing $\lambda_n$.
